site.name: lumen-research
site.summary: Lumen Research — research assistant (local demo) Fictional research-assistant chat product. Local fixture for UXBench. Open `index.html` directly. Page `index.html` — Research thread Three-column layout: left rail for thread history, center conversation, right rail for Sources. Center column: - Conversation styled with serif body type. Each assistant turn renders inline citations as small chips (`[1]`, `[2]` …). Hovering a citation highlights and scrolls the matching source on the right; clicking jumps to it. - Embedded tables and lists are styled with the rest of the conversation.

run_plan.goal: Exhaustively explore and critique the UX of the Lumen Research chatbot interface, validating the primary conversation flow, citation interactions, thread management, and mode switching across desktop and mobile viewports.
run_plan.summary: The exploration will proceed by first validating the primary chat interface and citation interactions on the default thread. Next, it will test thread management by switching between existing threads and creating a new one. The run will then validate utility features like mode switching, sorting sources, and export options. Finally, all critical paths will be re-validated on a mobile viewport to assess responsive behavior and tap target issues identified in the prescan.
assumptions: The application is a local demo with simulated responses and no backend, so chat submissions will trigger scripted or no-op responses.
The right rail 'Sources' panel updates dynamically based on the active thread or selected mode.
Clicking 'Export as PDF' and 'Share thread' will attempt a browser action or trigger a mock UI state.
The left rail thread list is navigable and updates the center and right columns when a different thread is clicked.
risk_hotspots: Inline citation chips ([1], [2]) hover/click interactions failing to highlight or scroll the right rail Sources panel
Mode selector (ux-14) missing an accessible label (aria-label), causing screen reader failures
Left rail thread links (ux-2 to ux-11) having small tap targets (height < 44px) which will likely cause severe usability issues on mobile
Responsive layout of the three-column design potentially collapsing poorly or hiding essential controls on mobile viewports

phases.title: Primary Chat & Citation Flow
phases.objective: Validate the core conversation experience, including reading the thread, interacting with inline citations, and submitting a follow-up.
key_checks: Hover over inline citation chips (e.g., [1], [2]) and verify the matching source highlights in the right rail
Click an inline citation chip and verify the right rail scrolls to the specific source
Type a follow-up question in the textarea (ux-16) and submit using the Ask button (ux-18)
Click the suggested follow-up buttons (e.g., ux-19, ux-20) and verify system response
exit_criteria: Citation hover and click behaviors are confirmed
A follow-up question and a suggested prompt have been successfully submitted

phases.title: Thread Navigation & Creation
phases.objective: Validate the left rail thread history navigation and the creation of a new thread.
key_checks: Click a different thread in the left rail (e.g., 'EV battery recycling policy in Norway') and verify center and right columns update
Click the '+ New thread' button (ux-1) and verify the interface resets for a new conversation
Submit an initial query in the new thread to test the blank state
Verify the new thread appears in the left rail history
exit_criteria: Successfully navigated between at least two existing threads
Successfully created a new thread and submitted a query

phases.title: Modes, Sources & Utilities
phases.objective: Validate the functionality of the mode selector, source sorting, and utility actions (Share, Export, Attach).
key_checks: Change the Mode selector (ux-14) to 'Quick scan', 'Deep dive', and 'Compare arguments', observing changes in the UI/response
Change the Sort dropdown (ux-23) to 'Date' and 'Cited in this answer', verifying source order changes in the right rail
Click the 'All' button (ux-24) in the right rail and verify filter behavior
Click 'Share thread' (ux-12) and 'Export as PDF' (ux-13) to check for expected dialogs or actions
Click the attachment button (ux-15) to check file picker or mock response
exit_criteria: All mode and sort options have been exercised
Utility buttons (Share, Export, Attach) have been clicked and their outcomes observed

phases.title: Mobile Viewport Validation
phases.objective: Re-validate critical flows and assess responsive layout on a mobile viewport, paying special attention to tap targets and three-column collapse behavior.
key_checks: Switch to mobile viewport and verify the three-column layout adapts (e.g., left rail collapses to hamburger or hidden)
Attempt to navigate thread history on mobile, checking for tap target issues flagged in prescan
Validate citation hover/click interaction on mobile (tap instead of hover)
Submit a follow-up question on mobile
Access Mode selector and Sort dropdown on mobile
exit_criteria: Mobile layout is assessed for usability and responsive integrity
Critical chat and citation flows are confirmed functional on mobile
Tap target severity is evaluated in context

coverage_targets.features: Exercise all 14 buttons, 4 inputs/selects, and 10 links identified in the prescan
coverage_targets.mobile: Repeat Phase 1 and Phase 2 critical checks on mobile viewport, plus validate layout collapse

notes: The prescan flagged 11 small tap targets in the left rail; mobile testing should specifically evaluate if these links are hidden behind a menu or remain difficult to tap.
The mode selector (ux-14) is missing an accessible label; verify if this impacts visual usability or is purely an accessibility (a11y) concern.

observation.title: Lumen Research — research assistant
observation.visible_text: Lumen + New thread TODAY Deep work scheduling literature EV battery recycling policy in Norway Trace prevalence of seal influenza H10N7 LAST 7 DAYS Comparative grad-school stipends in CS Microclimate effects of urban rooftop gardens Late-Holocene shoreline shifts, NW Europe Why does ringing happen in step responses EARLIER Survey: open-source funding models 2024 Caffeine half-life in slow metabolizers Building codes vs wildfire defensible space PA Priya Anand Researcher · Pro Deep work scheduling literature Share thread Export as PDF Mode: Balanced Mode: Quick scan Mode: Deep dive Mode: Compare arguments Hi — I'm planning a 6-week study on whether "two 90-minute deep-work blocks before noon" actually outperform afternoon-heavy schedules for software engineers. What does the existing literature say about this? L Short version: there's strong general support for protected morning blocks in attention-heavy work, but the specific comparison you're describing — two 90-minute blocks before noon vs. afternoon-heavy — has thin direct evidence and a lot of confounded chronotype work nearby. Here's how the field breaks down. Cognitive performance peaks vary by chronotype. Roughly 30% of working adults are "owls," for whom afternoon blocks aren't a deficit [1]. Pre-noon-heavy schedules show their largest effect for morning and intermediate types [2]. Block length matters more than block start time. The 90-min figure traces back to Kleitman's basic-rest-activity-cycle work and Ericsson's deliberate-practice studies; both argue for ~90-minute bouts, but neither pins them to morning [3]. The strongest field study I can find is Newport & Hempel's 2022 review of 11 industry interventions; protected blocks improved task completion by 18–32% regardless of time of day [4]. If you want a cleanly testable design, I'd recommend isolating "morning-loading" from "block protection" — otherwise any effect will be confounded. I can sketch a 2×2 protocol if you'd like. Yes please, sketch the 2×2. And how would you measure "deep work" output beyond self-report? L Sketch of a within-subjects 2×2 design (each engineer rotates through all four conditions, two weeks each): Morning-loaded Afternoon-loaded Protected blocks A: 2×90 min, 9–12 B: 2×90 min, 1–4 Unprotected (control) C: Schedule yourself, mornings D: Schedule yourself, afternoons For output measures beyond self-report, you've got three credible options: Code-event telemetry — merged-PR count, mean time from "first edit" to "first commit," IDE focus-session length. Drawbacks: noisy at the daily level [5]. Peer-rated weekly delivery scores — bias-adjusted Likert from one rotating reviewer, blinded to condition [6]. Cognitive bandwidth probes — n-back at 4 PM, ostensibly unrelated but predictive of after-work fatigue [7]. The cleanest single measure is probably "Total focus-session minutes per workday" measured by IDE plugin — it sidesteps self-report and is easy to log. L Short version: there's strong general support for protected morning blocks in attention-heavy work, but the specific comparison you're describing — two 90-minute blocks before noon vs. afternoon-heavy — has thin direct evidence and a lot of confounded chronotype work nearby. observation.title: Lumen Research — research assistant
observation.visible_text: Lumen + New thread TODAY Deep work scheduling literature EV battery recycling policy in Norway Trace prevalence of seal influenza H10N7 LAST 7 DAYS Comparative grad-school stipends in CS Microclimate effects of urban rooftop gardens Late-Holocene shoreline shifts, NW Europe Why does ringing happen in step responses EARLIER Survey: open-source funding models 2024 Caffeine half-life in slow metabolizers Building codes vs wildfire defensible space PA Priya Anand Researcher · Pro Deep work scheduling literature Share thread Export as PDF Mode: Balanced Mode: Quick scan Mode: Deep dive Mode: Compare arguments Hi — I'm planning a 6-week study on whether "two 90-minute deep-work blocks before noon" actually outperform afternoon-heavy schedules for software engineers. What does the existing literature say about this? L Short version: there's strong general support for protected morning blocks in attention-heavy work, but the specific comparison you're describing — two 90-minute blocks before noon vs. afternoon-heavy — has thin direct evidence and a lot of confounded chronotype work nearby. Here's how the field breaks down. Cognitive performance peaks vary by chronotype. Roughly 30% of working adults are "owls," for whom afternoon blocks aren't a deficit [1]. Pre-noon-heavy schedules show their largest effect for morning and intermediate types [2]. Block length matters more than block start time. The 90-min figure traces back to Kleitman's basic-rest-activity-cycle work and Ericsson's deliberate-practice studies; both argue for ~90-minute bouts, but neither pins them to morning [3]. The strongest field study I can find is Newport & Hempel's 2022 review of 11 industry interventions; protected blocks improved task completion by 18–32% regardless of time of day [4]. If you want a cleanly testable design, I'd recommend isolating "morning-loading" from "block protection" — otherwise any effect will be confounded. I can sketch a 2×2 protocol if you'd like. Yes please, sketch the 2×2. And how would you measure "deep work" output beyond self-report? L Sketch of a within-subjects 2×2 design (each engineer rotates through all four conditions, two weeks each): Morning-loaded Afternoon-loaded Protected blocks A: 2×90 min, 9–12 B: 2×90 min, 1–4 Unprotected (control) C: Schedule yourself, mornings D: Schedule yourself, afternoons For output measures beyond self-report, you've got three credible options: Code-event telemetry — merged-PR count, mean time from "first edit" to "first commit," IDE focus-session length. Drawbacks: noisy at the daily level [5]. Peer-rated weekly delivery scores — bias-adjusted Likert from one rotating reviewer, blinded to condition [6]. Cognitive bandwidth probes — n-back at 4 PM, ostensibly unrelated but predictive of after-work fatigue [7]. The cleanest single measure is probably "Total focus-session minutes per workday" measured by IDE plugin — it sidesteps self-report and is easy to log. Got it — give me one or two sentences I could put in the IRB proposal explaining why I'm not measuring "lines of code." L "Lines of code is a poor proxy for engineering output because it incentivizes verbosity and weakly correlates with task completion or code quality [8]. This study therefore measures protected focus-session minutes (from IDE telemetry) and bias-adjusted peer-rated weekly delivery, neither of which rewards code volume." What are the main confounding variables in chronotype studies? L Thinking out loud while I assemble sources… Here's a first pass. The most directly relevant body of work is the chronotype × intervention literature; I'll prioritize that and bring in a couple of negative results to keep the picture honest. I added 3 new sources to the panel on the right. Want me to dig into any of them in particular? 📎 Balanced Quick scan Deep dive Ask Follow-up questions Lumen suggests Find papers since 2020 directly comparing the two schedules Power analysis for 24 engineers × 2 weeks Surface negative results: where m

What does the existing literature say about this? L Short version: there's strong general support for protected morning blocks in attention-heavy work, but the specific comparison you're describing — two 90-minute blocks before noon vs. afternoon-heavy — has thin direct evidence and a lot of confounded chronotype work nearby. Here's how the field breaks down. Cognitive performance peaks vary by chronotype. Roughly 30% of working adults are "owls," for whom afternoon blocks aren't a deficit [1]. Pre-noon-heavy schedules show their largest effect for morning and intermediate types [2]. Block length matters more than block start time. The 90-min figure traces back to Kleitman's basic-rest-activity-cycle work and Ericsson's deliberate-practice studies; both argue for ~90-minute bouts, but neither pins them to morning [3]. The strongest field study I can find is Newport & Hempel's 2022 review of 11 industry interventions; protected blocks improved task completion by 18–32% regardless of time of day [4]. If you want a cleanly testable design, I'd recommend isolating "morning-loading" from "block protection" — otherwise any effect will be confounded. I can sketch a 2×2 protocol if you'd like. Cognitive bandwidth probes — n-back at 4 PM, ostensibly unrelated but predictive of after-work fatigue [7]. L "Lines of code is a poor proxy for engineering output because it incentivizes verbosity and weakly correlates with task completion or code quality [8]. This study therefore measures protected focus-session minutes (from IDE telemetry) and bias-adjusted peer-rated weekly delivery, neither of which rewards code volume." What are the main confounding variables in chronotype studies? L Thinking out loud while I assemble sources… Here's a first pass. The most directly relevant body of work is the chronotype × intervention literature; I'll prioritize that and bring in a couple of negative results to keep the picture honest. observation.title: Lumen Research — research assistant
observation.visible_text: Lumen + New thread TODAY Deep work scheduling literature EV battery recycling policy in Norway Trace prevalence of seal influenza H10N7 LAST 7 DAYS Comparative grad-school stipends in CS Microclimate effects of urban rooftop gardens Late-Holocene shoreline shifts, NW Europe Why does ringing happen in step responses EARLIER Survey: open-source funding models 2024 Caffeine half-life in slow metabolizers Building codes vs wildfire defensible space PA Priya Anand Researcher · Pro Deep work scheduling literature Share thread Export as PDF Mode: Balanced Mode: Quick scan Mode: Deep dive Mode: Compare arguments Hi — I'm planning a 6-week study on whether "two 90-minute deep-work blocks before noon" actually outperform afternoon-heavy schedules for software engineers. What does the existing literature say about this? L Short version: there's strong general support for protected morning blocks in attention-heavy work, but the specific comparison you're describing — two 90-minute blocks before noon vs. afternoon-heavy — has thin direct evidence and a lot of confounded chronotype work nearby. Here's how the field breaks down. Cognitive performance peaks vary by chronotype. Roughly 30% of working adults are "owls," for whom afternoon blocks aren't a deficit [1]. Pre-noon-heavy schedules show their largest effect for morning and intermediate types [2]. Block length matters more than block start time. The 90-min figure traces back to Kleitman's basic-rest-activity-cycle work and Ericsson's deliberate-practice studies; both argue for ~90-minute bouts, but neither pins them to morning [3]. The strongest field study I can find is Newport & Hempel's 2022 review of 11 industry interventions; protected blocks improved task completion by 18–32% regardless of time of day [4]. If you want a cleanly testable design, I'd recommend isolating "morning-loading" from "block protection" — otherwise any effect will be confounded. I can sketch a 2×2 protocol if you'd like. Yes please, sketch the 2×2. And how would you measure "deep work" output beyond self-report? L Sketch of a within-subjects 2×2 design (each engineer rotates through all four conditions, two weeks each): Morning-loaded Afternoon-loaded Protected blocks A: 2×90 min, 9–12 B: 2×90 min, 1–4 Unprotected (control) C: Schedule yourself, mornings D: Schedule yourself, afternoons For output measures beyond self-report, you've got three credible options: Code-event telemetry — merged-PR count, mean time from "first edit" to "first commit," IDE focus-session length. Drawbacks: noisy at the daily level [5]. Peer-rated weekly delivery scores — bias-adjusted Likert from one rotating reviewer, blinded to condition [6]. Cognitive bandwidth probes — n-back at 4 PM, ostensibly unrelated but predictive of after-work fatigue [7]. The cleanest single measure is probably "Total focus-session minutes per workday" measured by IDE plugin — it sidesteps self-report and is easy to log. Got it — give me one or two sentences I could put in the IRB proposal explaining why I'm not measuring "lines of code." L "Lines of code is a poor proxy for engineering output because it incentivizes verbosity and weakly correlates with task completion or code quality [8]. This study therefore measures protected focus-session minutes (from IDE telemetry) and bias-adjusted peer-rated weekly delivery, neither of which rewards code volume." What are the main confounding variables in chronotype studies? L Thinking out loud while I assemble sources… Here's a first pass. The most directly relevant body of work is the chronotype × intervention literature; I'll prioritize that and bring in a couple of negative results to keep the picture honest. I added 3 new sources to the panel on the right. Want me to dig into any of them in particular? 📎 Balanced Quick scan Deep dive Ask Follow-up questions Lumen suggests Find papers since 2020 directly comparing the two schedules Power analysis for 24 engineers × 2 weeks Surface negative results: where m

observation.visible_text: Lumen + New thread TODAY Deep work scheduling literature EV battery recycling policy in Norway Trace prevalence of seal influenza H10N7 LAST 7 DAYS Comparative grad-school stipends in CS Microclimate effects of urban rooftop gardens Late-Holocene shoreline shifts, NW Europe Why does ringing happen in step responses EARLIER Survey: open-source funding models 2024 Caffeine half-life in slow metabolizers Building codes vs wildfire defensible space PA Priya Anand Researcher · Pro Deep work scheduling literature Share thread Export as PDF Mode: Balanced Mode: Quick scan Mode: Deep dive Mode: Compare arguments Hi — I'm planning a 6-week study on whether "two 90-minute deep-work blocks before noon" actually outperform afternoon-heavy schedules for software engineers. What does the existing literature say about this? L Short version: there's strong general support for protected morning blocks in attention-heavy work, but the specific comparison you're describing — two 90-minute blocks before noon vs. afternoon-heavy — has thin direct evidence and a lot of confounded chronotype work nearby. Here's how the field breaks down. Cognitive performance peaks vary by chronotype. Roughly 30% of working adults are "owls," for whom afternoon blocks aren't a deficit [1]. Pre-noon-heavy schedules show their largest effect for morning and intermediate types [2]. Block length matters more than block start time. The 90-min figure traces back to Kleitman's basic-rest-activity-cycle work and Ericsson's deliberate-practice studies; both argue for ~90-minute bouts, but neither pins them to morning [3]. The strongest field study I can find is Newport & Hempel's 2022 review of 11 industry interventions; protected blocks improved task completion by 18–32% regardless of time of day [4]. If you want a cleanly testable design, I'd recommend isolating "morning-loading" from "block protection" — otherwise any effect will be confounded. I can sketch a 2×2 protocol if you'd like. Yes please, sketch the 2×2. And how would you measure "deep work" output beyond self-report? L Sketch of a within-subjects 2×2 design (each engineer rotates through all four conditions, two weeks each): Morning-loaded Afternoon-loaded Protected blocks A: 2×90 min, 9–12 B: 2×90 min, 1–4 Unprotected (control) C: Schedule yourself, mornings D: Schedule yourself, afternoons For output measures beyond self-report, you've got three credible options: Code-event telemetry — merged-PR count, mean time from "first edit" to "first commit," IDE focus-session length. Drawbacks: noisy at the daily level [5]. Peer-rated weekly delivery scores — bias-adjusted Likert from one rotating reviewer, blinded to condition [6]. Cognitive bandwidth probes — n-back at 4 PM, ostensibly unrelated but predictive of after-work fatigue [7]. The cleanest single measure is probably "Total focus-session minutes per workday" measured by IDE plugin — it sidesteps self-report and is easy to log. Got it — give me one or two sentences I could put in the IRB proposal explaining why I'm not measuring "lines of code." L "Lines of code is a poor proxy for engineering output because it incentivizes verbosity and weakly correlates with task completion or code quality [8]. This study therefore measures protected focus-session minutes (from IDE telemetry) and bias-adjusted peer-rated weekly delivery, neither of which rewards code volume." What are the main confounding variables in chronotype studies? L Thinking out loud while I assemble sources… Here's a first pass. The most directly relevant body of work is the chronotype × intervention literature; I'll prioritize that and bring in a couple of negative results to keep the picture honest. I added 3 new sources to the panel on the right. Want me to dig into any of them in particular? 📎 Balanced Quick scan Deep dive Ask Follow-up questions Lumen suggests Find papers since 2020 directly comparing the two schedules Power analysis for 24 engineers × 2 weeks Surface negative results: where m

observation.title: Lumen Research — research assistant
observation.visible_text: Lumen + New thread TODAY Deep work scheduling literature EV battery recycling policy in Norway Trace prevalence of seal influenza H10N7 LAST 7 DAYS Comparative grad-school stipends in CS Microclimate effects of urban rooftop gardens Late-Holocene shoreline shifts, NW Europe Why does ringing happen in step responses EARLIER Survey: open-source funding models 2024 Caffeine half-life in slow metabolizers Building codes vs wildfire defensible space PA Priya Anand Researcher · Pro Deep work scheduling literature Share thread Export as PDF Mode: Balanced Mode: Quick scan Mode: Deep dive Mode: Compare arguments Hi — I'm planning a 6-week study on whether "two 90-minute deep-work blocks before noon" actually outperform afternoon-heavy schedules for software engineers. What does the existing literature say about this? L Short version: there's strong general support for protected morning blocks in attention-heavy work, but the specific comparison you're describing — two 90-minute blocks before noon vs. afternoon-heavy — has thin direct evidence and a lot of confounded chronotype work nearby. Here's how the field breaks down. Cognitive performance peaks vary by chronotype. Roughly 30% of working adults are "owls," for whom afternoon blocks aren't a deficit [1]. Pre-noon-heavy schedules show their largest effect for morning and intermediate types [2]. Block length matters more than block start time. The 90-min figure traces back to Kleitman's basic-rest-activity-cycle work and Ericsson's deliberate-practice studies; both argue for ~90-minute bouts, but neither pins them to morning [3]. The strongest field study I can find is Newport & Hempel's 2022 review of 11 industry interventions; protected blocks improved task completion by 18–32% regardless of time of day [4]. If you want a cleanly testable design, I'd recommend isolating "morning-loading" from "block protection" — otherwise any effect will be confounded. I can sketch a 2×2 protocol if you'd like. Yes please, sketch the 2×2. And how would you measure "deep work" output beyond self-report? L Sketch of a within-subjects 2×2 design (each engineer rotates through all four conditions, two weeks each): Morning-loaded Afternoon-loaded Protected blocks A: 2×90 min, 9–12 B: 2×90 min, 1–4 Unprotected (control) C: Schedule yourself, mornings D: Schedule yourself, afternoons For output measures beyond self-report, you've got three credible options: Code-event telemetry — merged-PR count, mean time from "first edit" to "first commit," IDE focus-session length. Drawbacks: noisy at the daily level [5]. Peer-rated weekly delivery scores — bias-adjusted Likert from one rotating reviewer, blinded to condition [6]. Cognitive bandwidth probes — n-back at 4 PM, ostensibly unrelated but predictive of after-work fatigue [7]. The cleanest single measure is probably "Total focus-session minutes per workday" measured by IDE plugin — it sidesteps self-report and is easy to log. Got it — give me one or two sentences I could put in the IRB proposal explaining why I'm not measuring "lines of code." L "Lines of code is a poor proxy for engineering output because it incentivizes verbosity and weakly correlates with task completion or code quality [8]. This study therefore measures protected focus-session minutes (from IDE telemetry) and bias-adjusted peer-rated weekly delivery, neither of which rewards code volume." What are the main confounding variables in chronotype studies? L Thinking out loud while I assemble sources… Here's a first pass. The most directly relevant body of work is the chronotype × intervention literature; I'll prioritize that and bring in a couple of negative results to keep the picture honest. I added 3 new sources to the panel on the right. Want me to dig into any of them in particular? 📎 Balanced Quick scan Deep dive Ask Follow-up questions Lumen suggests Find papers since 2020 directly comparing the two schedules Power analysis for 24 engineers × 2 weeks Surface negative results: where m

What does the existing literature say about this? L Short version: there's strong general support for protected morning blocks in attention-heavy work, but the specific comparison you're describing — two 90-minute blocks before noon vs. afternoon-heavy — has thin direct evidence and a lot of confounded chronotype work nearby. Here's how the field breaks down. Cognitive performance peaks vary by chronotype. Roughly 30% of working adults are "owls," for whom afternoon blocks aren't a deficit [1]. Pre-noon-heavy schedules show their largest effect for morning and intermediate types [2]. Block length matters more than block start time. L "Lines of code is a poor proxy for engineering output because it incentivizes verbosity and weakly correlates with task completion or code quality [8]. L Short version: there's strong general support for protected morning blocks in attention-heavy work, but the specific comparison you're describing — two 90-minute blocks before noon vs. afternoon-heavy — has thin direct evidence and a lot of confounded chronotype work nearby. Here's how the field breaks down. Cognitive performance peaks vary by chronotype. Roughly 30% of working adults are "owls," for whom afternoon blocks aren't a deficit [1]. Pre-noon-heavy schedules show their largest effect for morning and intermediate types [2]. Block length matters more than block start time. The 90-min figure traces back to Kleitman's basic-rest-activity-cycle work and Ericsson's deliberate-practice studies; both argue for ~90-minute bouts, but neither pins them to morning [3]. The strongest field study I can find is Newport & Hempel's 2022 review of 11 industry interventions; protected blocks improved task completion by 18–32% regardless of time of day [4]. If you want a cleanly testable design, I'd recommend isolating "morning-loading" from "block protection" — otherwise any effect will be confounded. I can sketch a 2×2 protocol if you'd like. Yes please, sketch the 2×2. And how would you measure "deep work" output beyond self-report? L Sketch of a within-subjects 2×2 design (each engineer rotates through all four conditions, two weeks each): Morning-loaded Afternoon-loaded Protected blocks A: 2×90 min, 9–12 B: 2×90 min, 1–4 Unprotected (control) C: Schedule yourself, mornings D: Schedule yourself, afternoons For output measures beyond self-report, you've got three credible options: Code-event telemetry — merged-PR count, mean time from "first edit" to "first commit," IDE focus-session length. Drawbacks: noisy at the daily level [5]. Peer-rated weekly delivery scores — bias-adjusted Likert from one rotating reviewer, blinded to condition [6]. Cognitive bandwidth probes — n-back at 4 PM, ostensibly unrelated but predictive of after-work fatigue [7]. The cleanest single measure is probably "Total focus-session minutes per workday" measured by IDE plugin — it sidesteps self-report and is easy to log. Got it — give me one or two sentences I could put in the IRB proposal explaining why I'm not measuring "lines of code." L "Lines of code is a poor proxy for engineering output because it incentivizes verbosity and weakly correlates with task completion or code quality [8]. This study therefore measures protected focus-session minutes (from IDE telemetry) and bias-adjusted peer-rated weekly delivery, neither of which rewards code volume." 📎 Balanced Quick scan Deep dive Ask Follow-up questions Lumen suggests Find papers since 2020 directly comparing the two schedules Power analysis for 24 engineers × 2 weeks Surface negative results: where mornings didn't help Walk me through pre-registering on OSF Sources 8 Sort: Relevance Sort: Date Sort: Cited in this answer All Papers Books Web Preprints N Chronotype distribution in working adults — a meta-analysis Nature Sci Reports · 2021 · Olszewski et al. 0.88 "...approximately 31% of respondents in industrialized settings scored as evening-type or strongly evening-type, with mean peak alertnes

observation.title: Lumen Research — research assistant
observation.visible_text: Deep work scheduling literature Share thread Export as PDF Mode: Balanced Mode: Quick scan Mode: Deep dive Mode: Compare arguments Hi — I'm planning a 6-week study on whether "two 90-minute deep-work blocks before noon" actually outperform afternoon-heavy schedules for software engineers. What does the existing literature say about this? L Short version: there's strong general support for protected morning blocks in attention-heavy work, but the specific comparison you're describing — two 90-minute blocks before noon vs. afternoon-heavy — has thin direct evidence and a lot of confounded chronotype work nearby. Here's how the field breaks down. Cognitive performance peaks vary by chronotype. Roughly 30% of working adults are "owls," for whom afternoon blocks aren't a deficit [1]. Pre-noon-heavy schedules show their largest effect for morning and intermediate types [2]. Block length matters more than block start time. The 90-min figure traces back to Kleitman's basic-rest-activity-cycle work and Ericsson's deliberate-practice studies; both argue for ~90-minute bouts, but neither pins them to morning [3]. The strongest field study I can find is Newport & Hempel's 2022 review of 11 industry interventions; protected blocks improved task completion by 18–32% regardless of time of day [4]. If you want a cleanly testable design, I'd recommend isolating "morning-loading" from "block protection" — otherwise any effect will be confounded. I can sketch a 2×2 protocol if you'd like. Yes please, sketch the 2×2. And how would you measure "deep work" output beyond self-report? L Sketch of a within-subjects 2×2 design (each engineer rotates through all four conditions, two weeks each): Morning-loaded Afternoon-loaded Protected blocks A: 2×90 min, 9–12 B: 2×90 min, 1–4 Unprotected (control) C: Schedule yourself, mornings D: Schedule yourself, afternoons For output measures beyond self-report, you've got three credible options: Code-event telemetry — merged-PR count, mean time from "first edit" to "first commit," IDE focus-session length. Drawbacks: noisy at the daily level [5]. Peer-rated weekly delivery scores — bias-adjusted Likert from one rotating reviewer, blinded to condition [6]. Cognitive bandwidth probes — n-back at 4 PM, ostensibly unrelated but predictive of after-work fatigue [7]. The cleanest single measure is probably "Total focus-session minutes per workday" measured by IDE plugin — it sidesteps self-report and is easy to log. Got it — give me one or two sentences I could put in the IRB proposal explaining why I'm not measuring "lines of code." L "Lines of code is a poor proxy for engineering output because it incentivizes verbosity and weakly correlates with task completion or code quality [8]. This study therefore measures protected focus-session minutes (from IDE telemetry) and bias-adjusted peer-rated weekly delivery, neither of which rewards code volume." 📎 Balanced Quick scan Deep dive Ask Follow-up questions Lumen suggests Find papers since 2020 directly comparing the two schedules Power analysis for 24 engineers × 2 weeks Surface negative results: where mornings didn't help Walk me through pre-registering on OSF Sources 8 Sort: Relevance Sort: Date Sort: Cited in this answer All Papers Books Web Preprints N Chronotype distribution in working adults — a meta-analysis Nature Sci Reports · 2021 · Olszewski et al. 0.88 "...approximately 31% of respondents in industrialized settings scored as evening-type or strongly evening-type, with mean peak alertness occurring after 14:00." observation.title: Lumen Research — research assistant
observation.visible_text: Deep work scheduling literature Share thread Export as PDF Mode: Balanced Mode: Quick scan Mode: Deep dive Mode: Compare arguments Hi — I'm planning a 6-week study on whether "two 90-minute deep-work blocks before noon" actually outperform afternoon-heavy schedules for software engineers. What does the existing literature say about this? L Short version: there's strong general support for protected morning blocks in attention-heavy work, but the specific comparison you're describing — two 90-minute blocks before noon vs. afternoon-heavy — has thin direct evidence and a lot of confounded chronotype work nearby. Here's how the field breaks down. Cognitive performance peaks vary by chronotype. Roughly 30% of working adults are "owls," for whom afternoon blocks aren't a deficit [1]. Pre-noon-heavy schedules show their largest effect for morning and intermediate types [2]. Block length matters more than block start time. The 90-min figure traces back to Kleitman's basic-rest-activity-cycle work and Ericsson's deliberate-practice studies; both argue for ~90-minute bouts, but neither pins them to morning [3]. The strongest field study I can find is Newport & Hempel's 2022 review of 11 industry interventions; protected blocks improved task completion by 18–32% regardless of time of day [4]. If you want a cleanly testable design, I'd recommend isolating "morning-loading" from "block protection" — otherwise any effect will be confounded. I can sketch a 2×2 protocol if you'd like. Yes please, sketch the 2×2. And how would you measure "deep work" output beyond self-report? L Sketch of a within-subjects 2×2 design (each engineer rotates through all four conditions, two weeks each): Morning-loaded Afternoon-loaded Protected blocks A: 2×90 min, 9–12 B: 2×90 min, 1–4 Unprotected (control) C: Schedule yourself, mornings D: Schedule yourself, afternoons For output measures beyond self-report, you've got three credible options: Code-event telemetry — merged-PR count, mean time from "first edit" to "first commit," IDE focus-session length. Drawbacks: noisy at the daily level [5]. Peer-rated weekly delivery scores — bias-adjusted Likert from one rotating reviewer, blinded to condition [6]. Cognitive bandwidth probes — n-back at 4 PM, ostensibly unrelated but predictive of after-work fatigue [7]. The cleanest single measure is probably "Total focus-session minutes per workday" measured by IDE plugin — it sidesteps self-report and is easy to log. Got it — give me one or two sentences I could put in the IRB proposal explaining why I'm not measuring "lines of code." L "Lines of code is a poor proxy for engineering output because it incentivizes verbosity and weakly correlates with task completion or code quality [8]. This study therefore measures protected focus-session minutes (from IDE telemetry) and bias-adjusted peer-rated weekly delivery, neither of which rewards code volume." 📎 Balanced Quick scan Deep dive Ask Follow-up questions Lumen suggests Find papers since 2020 directly comparing the two schedules Power analysis for 24 engineers × 2 weeks Surface negative results: where mornings didn't help Walk me through pre-registering on OSF Sources 8 Sort: Relevance Sort: Date Sort: Cited in this answer All Papers Books Web Preprints N Chronotype distribution in working adults — a meta-analysis Nature Sci Reports · 2021 · Olszewski et al. 0.88 "...approximately 31% of respondents in industrialized settings scored as evening-type or strongly evening-type, with mean peak alertness occurring after 14:00." observation.title: Lumen Research — research assistant
observation.visible_text: Deep work scheduling literature Share thread Export as PDF Mode: Balanced Mode: Quick scan Mode: Deep dive Mode: Compare arguments Hi — I'm planning a 6-week study on whether "two 90-minute deep-work blocks before noon" actually outperform afternoon-heavy schedules for software engineers. What does the existing literature say about this? L Short version: there's strong general support for protected morning blocks in attention-heavy work, but the specific comparison you're describing — two 90-minute blocks before noon vs. afternoon-heavy — has thin direct evidence and a lot of confounded chronotype work nearby. Here's how the field breaks down. Cognitive performance peaks vary by chronotype. Roughly 30% of working adults are "owls," for whom afternoon blocks aren't a deficit [1]. Pre-noon-heavy schedules show their largest effect for morning and intermediate types [2]. Block length matters more than block start time. The 90-min figure traces back to Kleitman's basic-rest-activity-cycle work and Ericsson's deliberate-practice studies; both argue for ~90-minute bouts, but neither pins them to morning [3]. The strongest field study I can find is Newport & Hempel's 2022 review of 11 industry interventions; protected blocks improved task completion by 18–32% regardless of time of day [4]. If you want a cleanly testable design, I'd recommend isolating "morning-loading" from "block protection" — otherwise any effect will be confounded. I can sketch a 2×2 protocol if you'd like. Yes please, sketch the 2×2. And how would you measure "deep work" output beyond self-report? L Sketch of a within-subjects 2×2 design (each engineer rotates through all four conditions, two weeks each): Morning-loaded Afternoon-loaded Protected blocks A: 2×90 min, 9–12 B: 2×90 min, 1–4 Unprotected (control) C: Schedule yourself, mornings D: Schedule yourself, afternoons For output measures beyond self-report, you've got three credible options: Code-event telemetry — merged-PR count, mean time from "first edit" to "first commit," IDE focus-session length. Drawbacks: noisy at the daily level [5]. Peer-rated weekly delivery scores — bias-adjusted Likert from one rotating reviewer, blinded to condition [6]. Cognitive bandwidth probes — n-back at 4 PM, ostensibly unrelated but predictive of after-work fatigue [7]. The cleanest single measure is probably "Total focus-session minutes per workday" measured by IDE plugin — it sidesteps self-report and is easy to log. Got it — give me one or two sentences I could put in the IRB proposal explaining why I'm not measuring "lines of code." L "Lines of code is a poor proxy for engineering output because it incentivizes verbosity and weakly correlates with task completion or code quality [8]. This study therefore measures protected focus-session minutes (from IDE telemetry) and bias-adjusted peer-rated weekly delivery, neither of which rewards code volume." 📎 Balanced Quick scan Deep dive Ask Follow-up questions Lumen suggests Find papers since 2020 directly comparing the two schedules Power analysis for 24 engineers × 2 weeks Surface negative results: where mornings didn't help Walk me through pre-registering on OSF Sources 8 Sort: Relevance Sort: Date Sort: Cited in this answer All Papers Books Web Preprints N Chronotype distribution in working adults — a meta-analysis Nature Sci Reports · 2021 · Olszewski et al. 0.88 "...approximately 31% of respondents in industrialized settings scored as evening-type or strongly evening-type, with mean peak alertness occurring after 14:00." J Time-of-day effects in software-engineering productivity studies: a systematic review JSS · 2023 · Holm, Pereira, Boateng 0.84 "Effects of morning-loaded scheduling concentrate among morning and intermediate chronotypes; for evening types the same intervention is either neutral (k=4) or counter-productive (k=2)." B The BRAC and 90-minute work bouts — a historical reading Book chapter · 2019 · Tahir 0.72 "Kleitman's original BRAC observations describ
